question: How much does late delivery cost in customer review scores, and where do the late orders come from (seller-to-customer routes, states, categories, time)?

kpis.label: Delivered orders that arrived late
kpis.definition: Share of delivered orders whose delivery date (calendar day) is after the estimated delivery date.

kpis.label: Median arrival vs estimate
kpis.definition: Median of delivered date minus estimated date over delivered orders. Negative means early.

kpis.label: Average review, on time or early
kpis.definition: Mean review score of delivered orders that were not late, using the latest review per order.

kpis.label: Average review, late
kpis.definition: Mean review score of late delivered orders, using the latest review per order.

kpis.label: Late orders with a 1-star review
kpis.definition: Share of reviewed late orders scored 1, against 6.8% for on-time orders.

kpis.label: Late orders on the SP → RJ route
kpis.definition: Share of all late orders whose primary seller is in São Paulo and customer in Rio de Janeiro. The route carries 8.5% of delivered orders.

kpis.label: Worst month for late deliveries
kpis.definition: Highest monthly late rate by purchase month, 2017-01 to 2018-08.

kpis.label: Customers who bought again
kpis.definition: Share of customers (customer_unique_id) with delivered orders on two or more different purchase days.

findings.title: Late orders score about two stars lower
findings.summary: Late orders averaged 2.26 stars against 4.28 for orders that arrived on time or early. 54.2% of late orders got a 1-star review, compared with 6.8% of on-time orders.
findings.metric: Mean review score (1-5) and share of 1-star reviews; latest review per order; delivered orders.
findings.caveat: This is an association. Comparing late and on-time orders inside the same customer state, category or seller gives almost the same gap (-2.01, -2.02 and -1.98 stars), but other differences between late and on-time orders are not controlled.

findings.title: Estimates are generous, yet some orders still miss them
findings.summary: The median delivered order arrived 12 days before its estimate and 79% arrived at least a week early. Even so, 6.8% arrived after the estimated day.
findings.metric: Delivered date minus estimated date in whole days; late = positive.
findings.caveat: Comparing timestamps instead of dates would put the late rate at 8.1%, because estimates are stored at midnight. I use calendar days.

findings.title: One route accounts for about a sixth of late orders
findings.summary: Orders shipped from São Paulo to Rio de Janeiro were 8.5% of delivered orders but 17.6% of late ones, with a late rate of 14.1% (95% interval 13.4% to 14.9%). No product category comes close: the largest excess over the average late rate for any category is 64 orders, against 600 for this route.
findings.metric: Late orders and late rate by route (primary seller state to customer state), Wilson 95% intervals.
findings.caveat: The dataset has no carrier or shipping-method fields, so route stands in for distance, carrier network and local conditions together. I can't separate them here.

findings.title: Four months produced over half of all late orders
findings.summary: Purchases from November-December 2017 and February-March 2018 were 27% of delivered orders but 55% of late ones; the late rate reached 12.4% in November 2017 and 19.0% in Mar 2018. In February and March 2018 carrier transit averaged 13.2 days against 8.6 in April and May, while seller handling time barely changed.
findings.metric: Late rate by purchase month; average days from purchase to carrier hand-off and from hand-off to delivery.
findings.caveat: November 2017 includes Black Friday volume. Nothing in the data names a cause for February and March 2018, and the last months are cut off by the end of the data, so they may look better than they were.

findings.title: Most late orders were reviewed before they arrived
findings.summary: 70% of reviews on late orders were answered before the recorded delivery time. For these orders the score was given while the customer was still waiting.
findings.metric: Share of late orders whose review answer timestamp is earlier than the delivery timestamp.
findings.caveat: The dataset describes when surveys were sent but not what triggered them. What it does show is that 91% of 1- and 2-star reviews on late orders were given before the product arrived.

findings.title: Very few customers come back, late or not
findings.summary: Only 2.2% of customers with a delivered order bought again on a later day. Customers whose first order was late came back within 180 days at 1.6%, against 2.0% after an on-time first order.
findings.metric: Customers by customer_unique_id; repeat = delivered orders on two or more purchase days.
findings.caveat: The intervals overlap (1.2% to 2.0% vs 1.9% to 2.1%), so the data can't show whether lateness changes repeat buying.

statistics.note: Welch t-test and a normal-approximation interval for the 1-star gap. Descriptive; not causal.

next_steps: Review how delivery estimates are set for routes into Rio de Janeiro and the Northeast, where late rates are well above the average, and test any change on a small share of orders first.
Track the late rate weekly by route with a simple alert threshold, so a spike like February and March 2018 shows up within days.
Test holding the review request until an order is delivered, or asking about delivery separately, so seller and product ratings are not mixed with delivery delays.
Add carrier and shipping-method data to the model, since without it I can't tell carrier performance apart from distance.
